receipt.public_excerpt: Since May 1, judges have called out at least 23 examples of AI hallucinations in court records.

evidence_items.explanation: At least 23 separate court findings in under four weeks of May 2025, nearly one a day. That is a regular pattern, not an anomaly.

receipt.public_excerpt: last month, legal professionals were found to be at fault in at least 13 of 23 cases where AI errors were found.

evidence_items.explanation: Lawyers and other legal professionals were at fault in at least 13 of the 23 May 2025 cases. This backs the claim's focus on lawyers.

receipt.public_excerpt: In a decision filed May 6, retired U.S. Magistrate Judge Michael R. Wilner of the Central District of California imposed the monetary penalty, struck the deficient brief, and barred further discovery on the issue that it addressed.

evidence_items.explanation: A dated May 2025 example: a court sanctioned two established law firms (K&L Gates and Ellis George) over a brief with AI-fabricated authorities. Even large firms were affected.

receipt.public_excerpt: “Before this spring in 2025, we maybe had two cases per week,” said Charlotin, the French researcher who tracks such cases. “Now we’re at two cases per day or three cases per day.”

evidence_items.explanation: Charlotin, who keeps the database, describes a steady pace before spring 2025 that later sped up. This is context only, since it was said in October 2025.

unresolved_gaps: I did not count the May 2025 entries in Charlotin's database directly. The current page lists recent 2026 cases, so the May 2025 count rests on Business Insider's reading of the database.
The database counts only cases where a court flagged the problem. The true number of AI-made-up citations, and their share of all filings, is unknown.
